newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FRENCH POLICY STANCE SEEN UNDERMINING EMU CRITERIA.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH POLICY STANCE SEEN UNDERMINING EMU CRITERIA.

text.p: The inherent contradictions in French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's economic policy programme have put a spotlight on the entry criteria for a single European currency, analysts say.

Appearing before the French parliament on Thursday, Jospin outlined what many perceive as a relatively ambitious list of spending initiatives, designed to tackle France's stubbornly high unemployment rate.

What analysts found most troubling about Jospin's speech was the lack of any reference to the Maastricht Treaty's requirement that budget deficits for 1997 must be close to three percent of Gross Domestic Product, or any indication of what he might do to close a widely expected revenue shortfall.

Jospin acknowledged that the government's fiscal situation looked "serious." Combining that observation with the renewed commitment to enter the single currency, many were left scratching their heads over how the new French prime minister plans to square the circle.

"There is now a question mark over the willingness of the French government to qualify for EMU," said Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney, who reckons France's public sector deficit could climb as high as 3.6 percent of GDP this year.

Throughout the EU, strict adherence to the Treaty's requirement that EMU aspirants must bring their deficits down to three percent of GDP looks increasingly unlikely given Germany's own difficulties in bringing expenditure under control.
But whether this implies that the EU is entering an anything-goes type of environment is far from agreed, with some reckoning that only a slight overshoot would be permitted.
Others, however, expect to see the Treaty's often vague and elusive language exploited to the maximum, with the emphasis on sustainable budgetary convergence taking on a new twist.
"The Treaty allows you to do everything and anything," said Susanne Schmidt, political analyst at the Daiwa Institute of Research Europe in London.
If France can demonstrate that its 1998 budget outlook is likely to improve versus 1997, then it might be able to meet the demands of durable budgetary convergence, adds Schmidt.
Moreover, there is the critical element of political will.
"I think in both countries (Germany and France) the political will is still very strong to let (EMU) happen on time, and if nothing else that's what that Amsterdam summit has shown."

Another important consideration in judging how EMU stays on track is the political dynamic between the relevant EU institutions that will make recommendations on membership and the final decision by heads of state.
While the ultimate judgment on who joins the euro will be made by EU leaders, they will be acting on opinions from the European Monetary Institute (EMI) and the European Commission.

It is no mystery that the Frankfurt-based EMI will likely take a relatively stern approach towards which countries meet the rigours of the Treaty. Unlike the Commission, which is more of a political animal, the EMI, forerunner to a European Central Bank, is under considerable pressure to demonstrate its independence from outside meddling.

Charles Goodhart, economist at the London School of Economics, and also a member of the Bank of England's monetary committee, says Jospin's inconsistencies resemble those of the former government except for the fact that there appears to be less concern over the Treaty's preconditions.
"The French are hoping the Maastricht deficit criterion will be gently ignored, but that raises the question of how Germany will react," Goodhart said.
If EU leaders override the views of the EMI, all sorts of uncertainties might open up, not least the reaction from the German public and its Constitutional Court.
"It's all far too uncertain to call," Goodhart added.
